newsitem.title: SPAIN: Fraud trial of spain's ex-civil guard chief starts.
newsitem.headline: Fraud trial of spain's ex-civil guard chief starts.

text.p: A corruption trial of former Civil Guard chief Luis Roldan, once Spain's most-wanted fugitive, began on Monday almost four years after the scandal exploded under the then-Socialist government.
Roldan and seven others, including his wife and a former girlfriend, are on trial for allegedly enriching themselves through kickbacks and by diverting secret government funds for personal use.

Roldan, the first civilian head of Spain's paramilitary Civil Guard, says he stashed money in Swiss bank accounts under his name and the name of family members on orders from Interior Ministry officials in order to supply Socialist party coffers.

"These served, in principle, to fight terrorism and then later to collect funds for the PSOE (Socialist Workers' Party)," Roldan told Madrid's provincial court, which was packed with journalists, during a two-hour appearance.
The ex-Civil Guard boss, who himself is a former Socialist, is seen by the party as a loose cannon who has fired off serious accusations against the previous Socialist administration.

He told the Supreme Court in May 1996 that former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez "knew everything" about a 1980s "dirty war" he said the Socialist government set up and ran against Basque separatist rebels.
Gonzalez has repeatedly denied any knowledge of the death squads that killed 28 supposed guerrillas from 1983-87. Party leaders say Roldan cannot be believed.

"Roldan has lost all credibility," Jesus Caldera, leader of the Socialist's parliamentary group, told journalists. "He's tried everything in his defence, like trying to implicate other PSOE members... but the public is able to discern that they were acts committed by an individual."
Wearing the same green suit he wore as a witness in several Socialist corruption cases, Roldan seemed nervous and spoke with a trace of irony in his first appearance as a defendant.

In 1995 before he could be formally charged, Roldan fled the country and was on the run for 10 months before being tracked down in Laos and extradited under circumstances that are still not entirely clear.
His flight was a serious embarrassment for Gonzalez' government, which was already hit by corruption scandals.

Roldan is charged with misuse of public funds, fraud, bribery, forgery, tax fraud and breach of duty. He faces a total 32 years of prison, 29 years of disqualification and 3.5 billion pesetas ($24 million) in fines.
The Socialists, which lost an election last year after nearly 14 years in power due in large part to the Roldan scandal, said they hoped he was given an "exemplary sentence".

"In order that those who defraud the citizens of Spain do not go unpunished," Caldera said. "The citizens of Spain want justice and the PSOE wants it and needs it... We have only one wish: that justice is done."

The trial, being held without television or radio and under tight security, started late for technical reasons and was then interrupted by a series of appeals and delaying tactics mounted by Roldan's defence.
Court sources said it could last five months.
